dryRun.title: An error thrown while rendering <Chart> inside <Boundary>
dryRun.note: An error boundary is a class component with static getDerivedStateFromError (and optionally componentDidCatch for logging). It catches errors from rendering and effects in the tree below it and shows a fallback instead of unmounting the whole app.

think.q:
class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null }
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error } }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <p>fallback: {this.state.error.message}</p> : this.props.children }
}
function Bad() { throw new Error('boom') }
why: The boundary shows its fallback; the rest of the page keeps working.

think.q:
class Boundary extends Component {
  state = { error: null }
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { error } }
  render() { return this.state.error ? <p>fallback: {this.state.error.message}</p> : this.props.children }
}
function Btn() { return <button onClick={() => { throw new Error('click') }}>x</button> }
why: Errors in event handlers are not caught by boundaries; React is not rendering at that moment. Catch them in the handler.

think.q: function Bad() { throw new Error('x') }
why: With no boundary, an uncaught render error unmounts the whole root: the user sees a blank page.

think.q: Where should error boundaries go?
opts: Around independent parts (a route, a widget, a chart) so one failure does not blank the page
why: Granularity decides how much of the UI a failure takes down.

think.q: A boundary shows a fallback for a user's profile. The user navigates to another profile. How do you clear the error?
opts: Give the boundary key={userId} so it remounts with fresh state
why: A new key means a new boundary instance.

try.task: Write ErrorBoundary taking fallback(error, reset) and onError(error) props: show fallback(error, reset) when a child throws while rendering, call onError once, and let reset() try rendering the children again.
try.hint: Class with state { error }, getDerivedStateFromError, componentDidCatch(error) → this.props.onError?.(error), reset = () => this.setState({ error: null }).

checks.t: shows the fallback and reports the error

takeaway.key: Error boundaries (a class with getDerivedStateFromError) catch render and effect errors below them. Event handlers and async code need try/catch. Reset with a key or a reset callback.
mistakes: One boundary for the whole app only.
Expecting boundaries to catch click-handler errors.

think.q: What must a modal rendered in a portal still do?
opts: Trap focus inside, close on Escape, return focus to the trigger, and mark the rest inert/aria-hidden
why: The native <dialog> element with showModal() handles much of this.

think.q: Why can't a tooltip inside a card with overflow: hidden simply use position: absolute?
opts: absolute is not allowed in React
It gets clipped by the card; a portal renders it outside that box
why: Portals escape clipping and stacking contexts.

try.task: Write Modal({ open, onClose, children }): when open, render via a portal into document.body a <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true"> with the children and a "Close" button; pressing Escape also calls onClose. Nothing is rendered when closed.
try.hint: if (!open) return null; useEffect adds a keydown listener on document while open (with cleanup); createPortal(…, document.body).

checks.t: renders into body via a portal
close button and Escape call onClose
renders nothing when closed and removes the key listener

takeaway.key: Portals move DOM elsewhere but keep the React tree: context and event bubbling still follow the component tree.
mistakes: Forgetting focus management in portal modals.
Being surprised that clicks in a portal bubble to React parents.

dryRun.title: Giving a parent access to a child's <input>
dryRun.note: Refs let a parent reach a DOM node or an imperative API of a child. In React 19, ref is a normal prop for function components, so forwardRef is no longer needed. useImperativeHandle exposes a small, deliberate API instead of the whole DOM node.

think.q:
function Input({ ref, ...p }) { return <input ref={ref} {...p} /> }
function App() { const r = useRef(null); useEffect(() => console.log(r.current.tagName), []); return <Input ref={r} /> }
why: React 19: ref is passed like any prop, no forwardRef needed.

think.q:
function Field({ ref }) { const inp = useRef(null); useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ clear: () => { inp.current.value = '' } })); return <input ref={inp} defaultValue="text" /> }
function App() { const r = useRef(null); return <><Field ref={r} /><button onClick={() => { console.log(Object.keys(r.current).join(), typeof r.current.focus); r.current.clear() }}>x</button></> }
why: The parent only gets what useImperativeHandle returns: clear, not the input's focus. And clear really emptied the field.

function App() { const r = useRef(null); return <><Field ref={r} /><button onClick={() => { console.log(Object.keys(r.current).join(), typeof r.current.focus); r.current.clear() }}>x</button></> }
await mount(<App />)
await click($('button'))
console.log(JSON.stringify($('input').value))

think.q: When is exposing a ref from a component appropriate?
opts: To read or change the child's state
Focus, scroll, select text, play/pause media: things that are naturally imperative
why: Data flows through props; refs are for imperative escape hatches.

think.q: You see forwardRef((props, ref) => …) in a React 19 codebase. Is it broken?
opts: No, it still works; it is just no longer required and may be deprecated later
why: New components can take ref as a prop.

think.q: A design-system Button should let parents focus it. Simplest React 19 way?
why: Pass the ref straight to the element.

try.task: Write SearchInput({ ref, ...props }) (React 19 style, no forwardRef) exposing only { focus(), clear() } through useImperativeHandle; clear also calls props.onClear?.().
try.hint: Keep an internal input ref; useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focus: () => inp.current.focus(), clear: () => { inp.current.value = ""; onClear?.() } })).

checks.t: clear empties it and calls onClear

takeaway.key: React 19: ref is a regular prop. Expose a small imperative API with useImperativeHandle; keep data in props.
mistakes: Using refs to push data into children.
Exposing the whole DOM node when two methods are enough.

dryRun.title: <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab id="a">A</Tabs.Tab></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel id="a">…</Tabs.Panel></Tabs>
rows: the active id (state), shares it through context
reads context; sets active on click
reads context; renders only if active
arranges the pieces freely in their own markup
dryRun.note: Compound components are a set of components that work together through a shared context, like <select> and <option>. The parent owns the state; the children read it. Users get a flexible API without dozens of props.

think.q:
const Ctx = createContext(null)
function Tabs({ children, initial }) { const [active, setActive] = useState(initial); return <Ctx value={{ active, setActive }}>{children}</Ctx> }
function Tab({ id, children }) { const c = useContext(Ctx); return <button onClick={() => c.setActive(id)}>{children}</button> }
function Panel({ id, children }) { return useContext(Ctx).active === id ? <p>{children}</p> : null }
why: The tab and the panel never talk directly; both read the shared context.

think.q:
const Ctx = createContext(null)
function Tab() { const c = useContext(Ctx); return <b>{c ? 'ok' : 'Tab must be inside Tabs'}</b> }
why: Outside the parent the context is null. Check it and throw a clear error in real code.

think.q: Main advantage over <Tabs tabs={[{ label, content }]} />?
opts: Users control the markup and order (add icons, wrap tabs, place panels anywhere) without new props
why: Config props grow forever; composition does not.

think.q: Which native HTML pair works like compound components?
why: The parent owns the selection; children declare options.

think.q: For tabs, what else should the pieces add?
why: Compound components are a good place to centralise a11y.

try.task: Build an Accordion with Accordion.Item, Accordion.Header and Accordion.Panel, sharing state through context. Only one item is open at a time; clicking an open header closes it.
examples: Header is a button with aria-expanded
try.hint: Accordion holds openId; Item provides its id with a second small context; Header toggles; Panel renders when open.

checks.t: clicking an open header closes it

takeaway.key: Compound components share state through context so users compose the pieces freely. Guard against use outside the parent.
mistakes: Pieces that crash with an unclear error outside their parent.

dryRun.title: <ApiProvider client={realClient}> in the app, <ApiProvider client={fakeClient}> in tests
dryRun.note: The provider pattern is dependency injection through context: something (an API client, a logger, feature flags) is created once at the top and read with a hook below. Components depend on the interface, not on how it was built.

think.q:
const Api = createContext(null)
const useApi = () => useContext(Api)
function Name() { return <p>{useApi().getUser().name}</p> }
why: The component uses whatever client the provider gives it.

think.q:
const Flags = createContext({})
function NewUI() { const f = useContext(Flags); return f.newCheckout ? <b>new</b> : <i>old</i> }
why: The nearest provider wins; outside any provider the default {} applies.

think.q: Biggest testing benefit of injecting an API client through a provider?
opts: Tests pass a fake client; no network mocking or module patching
why: Swap the dependency at the edge.

think.q: Ten nested providers in main.jsx feels messy. A reasonable fix?
opts: Compose them in one AppProviders component
Put all values in one giant context
why: One giant context re-renders everything on any change.

think.q: What should the value of a service provider usually be?
opts: Created once (module level, useState(() => …) or useMemo) so its identity is stable
why: Unstable values re-render every consumer.

try.task: Write ApiProvider({ client, children }) and useApi() (throws outside the provider), and a component UserName({ id }) that loads client.getUser(id) (a promise) in an effect and shows "Loading…" then the name.
try.hint: createContext(null); in UserName: useState(null) + useEffect with an ignore flag for cleanup.

checks.t: shows loading then the name from the injected client
a different client changes the result without touching the component

takeaway.key: Provide services (API clients, flags, loggers) once through context and read them with a guarded hook. Swap them in tests.
mistakes: Importing a real client directly inside components.

think.q: Why make ProductList presentational?
opts: It removes the need for state
You can render every state (loading, empty, error, full) in tests or Storybook without a server
why: Pure props → markup is the easiest code to test.

think.q: What usually replaces the "container component" today?
opts: A custom hook (useProducts) that returns { data, loading, error }
why: Same separation, less nesting.

think.q: When is this split overkill?
opts: For a tiny component used once with trivial data
why: Split when reuse or testing needs it.

think.q: A presentational DatePicker has an "open" flag for its popup. Is that allowed?
opts: No, presentational means no state at all
Yes: UI state that only matters inside the component can stay there
why: "Presentational" means no data fetching or app logic, not zero state.

try.task: Write a pure ProductList({ products, loading, error, onRetry }): "Loading…" while loading; an alert with the error and a Retry button; "No products" when empty; otherwise a list of name — ₹price.
try.hint: Early returns for each state, in order: loading, error, empty, list.

takeaway.key: Keep data logic (container or custom hook) apart from pure, prop-driven UI. Presentational components cover every state through props.
mistakes: Fetching inside deeply nested UI pieces.
Splitting tiny components for no reason.

think.q: What replaced most render props?
opts: Custom hooks: const { on, toggle } = useToggle()
why: Hooks share logic without extra nesting in JSX.

think.q: Classic downside of many render props?
opts: "Callback hell" nesting in JSX that is hard to read
why: Hooks flatten that nesting.

think.q: When is a render prop still a good choice?
opts: When the component also controls WHERE the custom content goes (e.g. a list calling renderItem per row)
why: renderItem in virtualized lists is a render prop.

try.task: Write List({ items, renderItem, renderEmpty }): renders a <ul> calling renderItem(item, index) for each item (wrapped in <li key>, key = item.id ?? index), or renderEmpty() (default: "Nothing here") when empty.

takeaway.key: A render prop is a function the component calls to render caller-defined UI with its state. Hooks replaced most uses; renderItem-style props remain useful.
mistakes: Forgetting keys on items rendered through a render prop.

dryRun.title: const AdminPage = withAuth(Page, { role: "admin" })
rows: wrapper hell, name clashes, hidden props
dryRun.note: A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra behaviour (auth checks, logging, injected data). Hooks replaced most HOCs, but you will see them in older code and libraries.

think.q:
function withUpper(C) { return function Wrapped(props) { return <C {...props} text={props.text.toUpperCase()} /> } }
function Label({ text }) { return <span>{text}</span> }
const Loud = withUpper(Label)
why: The HOC wraps Label and changes the prop before passing it on.

think.q:
function withNothing(C) { return function W() { return <C /> } }
function Show({ x }) { return <i>{String(x)}</i> }
const S = withNothing(Show)
why: The wrapper forgot to pass props through ({...props}), a classic HOC bug.

think.q:
function withLog(C) { function W(p) { return <C {...p} /> } W.displayName = `withLog(${C.name})`; return W }
function Card() { return null }
why: Set displayName so DevTools shows something readable.

think.q: Why must you never call withAuth(Page) inside a component's render?
opts: It creates a new component type every render, so React unmounts and remounts it (state lost)
why: Create HOC-wrapped components once at module level.

think.q: Modern alternative to withUser(Component)?
why: A hook gives the same data without wrapping.

try.task: Write withAuth(Component, { role }): returns a component that reads props.user; with no user render <p>Please log in</p>, with the wrong role <p>Forbidden</p>, else the Component with all props. Set a displayName.

checks.t: asks to log in without a user
renders the page with all props and a display name

takeaway.key: A HOC takes a component and returns an enhanced one. Pass all props through, set displayName, create it once. Prefer hooks in new code.
